lines.content: description: Apply the SE-EDU Git conventions when suggesting or creating commits and branches in this project.
Follow the SE-EDU Git conventions for this project:
- Write a clear subject line for every commit.
- Keep the subject near 50 characters where possible and under 72 characters.
- Use imperative mood, such as `Add JavaDoc comments`, not `Added JavaDoc`
- Capitalize the first letter of the subject.
- Do not end the subject with a period.
- For non-trivial commits, include a body separated from the subject by a blank
- Explain what changed and why it changed. Leave the exact implementation
details to the diff unless they are important context.
- Use meaningful branch names in kebab case.
- For CS2103T increment branches, preserve the assignment's requested names
when the user is following those instructions.
Do not commit, tag, or push unless the user explicitly asks for it.
description: Apply the SE-EDU Java coding standard to Java source and test code in this project.
Follow the SE-EDU Java coding standard for this project:
Use the Google Java Style Guide for topics not covered by SE-EDU.
- Put every class in a package under the project root package.
- Use lower-case package names and PascalCase class names.
- Use camelCase for variables and methods.
- Use boolean names that read like booleans, such as `isDone`, `hasTasks`,
- Use explicit imports. Do not use wildcard imports.
- Use 4 spaces for indentation and K&R braces.
- Initialize variables where declared when that keeps the value meaningful.
- Keep variables in the smallest reasonable scope.
- Wrap all conditionals and loops in braces.
- Write comments in English using American spelling and no local slang.
- Write JavaDoc header comments for public classes and public methods unless
the method is a getter/setter, an override whose parent JavaDoc applies
exactly, or test code where JavaDoc does not add value.
- For JavaDoc, use a short first sentence, include useful `@param`, `@return`,
and `@throws` tags, and end parameter descriptions with punctuation.

This repository is a starter template for a greenfield Java project used in an introductory software engineering course in an undergraduate computer science program. Students use it as the starting point for their own projects.

Unless the user says otherwise, assume that you are assisting a student working on a project in this repository. If the user identifies themselves as an instructor or another project stakeholder, adapt your response to that role.
* Prior knowledge: Basic Java and OOP concepts.
* Level of programming experience:  Beginner/intermediate; comfortable with basic Java syntax, still learning larger project structure and Git workflow.
* IDE and level of expertise: Some Intellij and VS code experience from previous course and projects, still learning more about IDE workflow
* Explain the rationale for significant actions: what you did and why.
* Keep explanations brief but instructive, supporting learning through responsible use of AI. For example:
* When suggesting a Git command, briefly explain what it does.
* Add explanatory Javadoc comments to all classes and to nontrivial methods and fields when their purpose or behavior is not obvious.
* Make generated code as self-explanatory as possible, and include explanatory comments where they improve understanding.
* When faced with a design choice, choose the simplest option that is sufficient for the requirements, while briefly explaining relevant more advanced alternatives.
Follow the project-specific skill `seedu-java-coding-standard` for all Java
source and test code in this repository.
Follow the project-specific skill `seedu-git-standard` whenever proposing or
creating commits, tags, branches, or Git history changes in this repository.
Ensure that Java 25 is used when running the application or build tasks. On macOS, use `sdk use java 25.0.3.fx-zulu` to switch to Java 25 if needed.
Use lightweight tags unless the user requests an annotated tag.
When proposing or creating a commit message, include enough detail to explain the rationale for the change.
Do not commit or push unless explicitly asked.

DisciTrack is a Java chatbot that helps users keep their discipline-related tasks on track. Given below are instructions on how to set up and run it.
Prerequisites: JDK 25, update IntelliJ to the most recent version.
1. Open IntelliJ (if you are not in the welcome screen, click `File` > `Close Project` to close the existing project first)
1. Open the project into IntelliJ as follows:
1. Select the project directory, and click `OK`.
1. If there are any further prompts, accept the defaults.
1. Configure the project to use **JDK 25** (not other versions) as explained in [here](https://www.jetbrains.com/help/idea/sdk.html#set-up-jdk).
In the same dialog, set the **Project language level** field to the `SDK default` option.

1. After that, locate the `src/main/java/DisciTrack.java` file, right-click it, and choose `Run DisciTrack.main()` (if the code editor is showing compile errors, try restarting the IDE). If the setup is correct, you should see the DisciTrack greeting in the output.

**Warning:** Keep the `src\main\java` folder as the root folder for Java files (i.e., don't rename those folders or move Java files to another folder outside of this folder path), as this is the default location some tools (e.g., Gradle) expect to find Java files.
